title: Dot products & the prediction equation
intro: This chapter is the mathematical foundation of the course. With a single ingredient — the dot product — you can describe exactly how every linear classifier makes predictions. Whoever understands this equation understands logistic regression and SVMs at the same time.

blocks.html: The dot product (inner product) of two vectors is: multiply them element-wise and add everything up. With x = [0, 1, 2] and y = [3, 4, 5] you get 0×3 = 0, 1×4 = 4 and 2×5 = 10, together \( 0 + 4 + 10 = 14 \). In Python (recent versions) you use the @ operator for this: x @ y. You can think of the dot product as multiplication in higher dimensions, since x and y are arrays of values.

blocks.label: dot product
blocks.caption: In numpy: x @ y — element-wise multiplication and summation.
The dot product in numpy
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

x = np.array([0, 1, 2])
y = np.array([3, 4, 5])

print('x * y (element-wise):', x * y)
print('sum of that         :', sum(x * y))
print('x @ y (dot product) :', x @ y)

sections.title: The prediction equation of linear classifiers

blocks.html:
Now the heart of the course. A linear classifier predicts in two steps. First it computes the raw model output: the dot product of the coefficients (the learned coef_) with the features, plus the intercept (the learned intercept_). Then it only looks at the sign: positive → the positive class, negative → the negative class.

Crucial insight: this pattern is identical for logistic regression and linear SVMs. In scikit-learn terms: different fit functions, the same predict function. The difference between the models therefore lies entirely in how they are fitted — those are the loss functions, later in this chapter.

blocks.label: raw model output
blocks.latex: f(x) \;=\; w \cdot x + b \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{p} w_i x_i + b
blocks.caption: w = coefficients (lr.coef_), b = intercept (lr.intercept_).

blocks.label: prediction
blocks.caption: Positive → positive class, negative → negative class (scikit-learn translates this into the class names of your data).
Rebuilding predict() yourself with coef_ and intercept_
blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
lr = LogisticRegression(max_iter=10000).fit(X, y)

for i in (10, 20):
    raw = lr.coef_ @ X[i] + lr.intercept_
    print(f'example {i:2d}: raw = {raw[0]:+8.3f}  '
          f'sign = {np.sign(raw[0]):+2.0f}  '
          f'lr.predict = {lr.predict([X[i]])[0]}')

blocks.html: See how predict does nothing but translate the sign of the raw model output back into class names (here 0 and 1). Same outcome, for every linear classifier.

sections.title: Seeing the boundary: coefficients and intercept steer it

blocks.html:
On the decision boundary itself the raw model output is exactly zero. Move away from the boundary on one side and the output becomes ever more negative; on the other side ever more positive. The sign therefore tells you on which side of the boundary you are — the magnitude tells you how far.

The value of b (intercept) shifts the boundary through space; change b and all raw outputs shift along. The coefficients w determine the orientation of the boundary: different coefficients, different direction of the line. This is literally what fit learns: the values of w and b that minimise the loss.

In 2D there are two coefficients while the direction of a line needs only one number. The ratio of the coefficients gives the direction of the boundary; the magnitude returns in chapter 3 as a measure of confidence.
